newsitem.title: USA: U.S. states efforts to limit heat oil rise mixed.
newsitem.headline: U.S. states efforts to limit heat oil rise mixed.

text.p: Amid the threat of the worst winter heating oil price squeeze in years, politicians are taking a closer look at efforts by three eastern U.S. state governments to limit the impact on their neediest citizens through hedging.

There is good news for those covered by the newest scheme, New Hampshire's pilot program which was launched in the summer. It locked in July heating oil prices for low income households, which has so far kept bills down by around $110 per person.
The bad news is it covers only around 2,700 people.

Just last week, a report by New York Attorney General Dennis Vacco recommended the exploration of state-directed futures purchases for home heat, to avert huge price spikes for people receiving assistance in paying their bills.

Heating oil's new prominence in regional politics comes after a rise of more than 50 pct in heating oil prices in the past four months. A new post-Gulf War high of 75.05 cents a gallon was set on the New York Mercantile (Futures) Exchange on Friday and further gains are forecast.

The Energy Department in Washington has said that though no actual shortage is expected, the price squeeze could go from bad to worse, depending on how cold the winter gets. Northeast politicians, with the world's biggest concentration of home heating oil users, have been calling for action.

Directors of the New Hampshire effort say they have been pushing their state government for seven years to try out a hedging program. But the extent of their success this year was largely down to luck and they recommend that hedging efforts should be kept simple.

"It was blind luck," said Richard Johnson, coordinator for New Hampshire's pilot program. "We locked in the price at (the low-point in July) through a pre-purchase plan at a guaranteed price. We didn't directly hedge; the dealers did on the New York Mercantile Exchange," Johnson said.

Johnson notes that in only one year out of the past 15 years have heating oil prices been higher in summer than in winter. "This is definitely a classic example of its advantages (of hedging)," he said.

The Massachusetts scheme, the oldest and largest hedging program, is far from simple. It has been in operation for six years and covers around 500,000 people. As well as a heating oil futures and options scheme, the state also buys forward physical natural gas and heating oil.

To get around federal laws prohibiting the direct involvement of state government in the futures and options market, the Massachusetts program is run through Citizens Energy Corp., founded with private money by Massachusetts congressman Joseph Kennedy. Citizens, in turn, employs investment bank Morgan Stanley to execute trades.
The state has had a mixed track record in getting prices down, said Steve Carvalho, deputy director for Massachusetts Bureau of Energy.
"Last year we purchased a million gallons in August (1995) for December heating oil. We were in the money as there was some price fluctuation," said Carvalho.
This year, however, there were delays in getting approval. By the time the state got the green light the cost of buying options contracts was judged prohibitive.

"The program didn't kick-off this year," said Carvalho. "In early August we looked at it but to lock-in for 69 cents (a gallon) for oil in January we would have been paying an eight cents premium. It was more of a gamble, and we decided not to do it this year."

Deleware mothballed its hedging program three years ago, according to David Truesdale, senior fiscal and policy analyst for the state budget office. "We stopped at that time because the oil market had become quite stable. Last winter we probably would have received some money back (if we hedged), but it's become too expensive," he said.
Also, the political urgency in Delaware has diminished as state-run buildings and operations have shifted away from heating oil to natural gas and electricity, said Truesdale.
